summary:
Farsight is an immersive, first-person lunar outpost survival simulation game that challenges players to restore a damaged lunar research station. Players take on the role of an astronaut responsible for maintaining critical life-support systems, including oxygen generation, water recycling, food production, power distribution, cooling, radiation protection, and communication systems.

The game features an explorable 3D lunar environment, interactive equipment, realistic resource-management challenges, and multiple repair-based mini-games. Players must prioritize repairs, manage limited resources and action points, and complete mission objectives to restore the outpost and establish communication with Earth.

Farsight combines space exploration, interactive learning, problem-solving, and simulation to introduce players to the technological challenges of sustaining human life on the Moon. It aims to make space science more engaging and accessible through an interactive gaming experience.
details:
What it does and how it works

The player is the commander of “Selene Base”, a lunar outpost near the south pole. A solar storm breaks power and radio, and the player must restore contact with the orbiting station and Earth.

The player walks through a 3D base: a central hub with four wings (power, greenhouse, life support, communications), plus the lunar surface outside.

Five meters (oxygen, power, water, food, crew safety) run from 0 to 100. If any reaches 0, the mission fails.

Each system is Working, Degraded or Failed. The player inspects a system to find its hidden fault, then repairs it through a short puzzle.

Each day gives about five actions. Repairs cost time, spare parts and power.

Nine random events (power fault, oxygen generator failure, solar particle event, and so on) change every run. Each is followed by a NASA-based fact.

The radio stays locked until the essential repairs are done, in a fixed order: generator, power distribution, life support, antenna, signal, then radio. The player does not need to fix everything.

Benefits and intended impact

Children feel why missions fail: power is shared, parts are limited, and one skipped repair causes later problems.

The end screen names the single biggest cause of a win or loss, so players learn from each run.

Real per-person figures (oxygen 0.84 kg, water 2.37 kg per day) and radiation data are sourced and shown on a Sources screen.

Tools

Three.js (3D) and cannon-es (physics), both MIT licensed. Plain JavaScript, so it runs in a browser from a link.

Antigravity as the editor. Claude helped with development.

Intro, ending and credits videos and the title image were made from scratch with scripts. Nothing uses NASA logos.

What is creative

It is a hands-on 3D base, not a menu game. You walk to the problem and fix it.

Repairs are puzzles, and dependencies between systems decide the order.

Random events differ each run, so there is replay value.

What we considered

Honest science: real values are labelled as real. Invented values (layout, repair costs, puzzle readings, mission length) are labelled as invented. ISS figures are never presented as lunar figures.

Real radiation is slow (about 7% of the 600 mSv career limit in 30 days). We speed it up in the game and tell the player.

The “dark side of the Moon” is a myth, so the game avoids that wording.

The game is designed so it cannot become unwinnable. Parts and power are always obtainable.

AI use is disclosed in the credits, on the Sources page and in the files.
